<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A survey experiment with 11 arms and a control group; online panel, United States. 2,257 responses were collected and 2,030 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A survey experiment on online panel respondents in United States (N = 2,030 analysed). Respondents are randomly assigned to 12 arms: Flagging, Provenance, Automated Flagging, AI Accuracy Nudge, Breathing Exercise, Mindfulness, Inoculation, AI Literacy Infographic, AI Literacy Infographic 2, AI Literacy Guide, AI Text Video, against the control group Control. Flagging: Posts in the feed are flagged as potentially AI-generated. Provenance: Posts carry information about the content's source and origin (provenance). Automated Flagging: Posts carry machine-learning-based AI-detection labels (automated flagging). AI Accuracy Nudge: Before the feed, an interactive task asks 'Is this image AI-generated?' (accuracy nudge). Breathing Exercise: Before the feed, a box-breathing exercise to reduce emotional reactivity. Mindfulness: Before the feed, a short mindfulness exercise. Inoculation: Before the feed, an inoculation message pre-exposing the respondent to manipulation techniques used in AI-generated media. AI Literacy Infographic: Before the feed, an infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Infographic 2: Before the feed, an alternative infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Guide: Before the feed, a comprehensive guide with examples of AI artifacts in images and videos. AI Text Video: Before the feed, an educational video about AI-generated text. Outcomes: Accuracy (share of 24 posts judged correctly), AI attitudes (opportunity vs threat, 6 items), Confidence in AI detection (single 7-point item), Trust in online information (7 items).


The study was registered on AsPredicted (#151,281, 2023-11-15). Some data existed at registration, but later batches followed the plan. Of 2,257 raw respondents, 2,030 entered the analysis (227 excluded; the exclusion criteria and the split by arm are not in the tables). Outcome models dropped a few rows with missing values, so some arm sizes fall slightly below eligible counts. The control group had 181 respondents. Arms were unbalanced, from 78 (Inoculation) to 333 (AI Accuracy Nudge). All tests are two-sided and uncorrected for multiple comparisons.

*Pre-registered.*

## Related work

Prior findings relevant to the study's hypotheses are limited and mostly indirect. Lewandowsky et al. (2017) and Wang et al. (2019) document that misinformation spreads widely and that people are poor at identifying false claims, providing general support for the premise that detection accuracy (H1) and trust in online information (H4) are malleable and in need of intervention. Pluviano et al. (2020) show that source expertise and trustworthiness cues shape recollection of misinformation, which is tangentially relevant to H1 and H4 but does not address AI-generated content specifically. No retrieved work directly examines interventions aimed at detecting AI-generated text or posts, so the list is thin for the study's core domain.

The most pointed disagreement in the retrieved set concerns whether individual-level interventions can meaningfully shift information-processing outcomes. Chater and Loewenstein (2022) argue that focusing on individual-level solutions has led behavioral public policy astray, implying that the study's design—targeting individual participants with brief interventions—may be insufficient to produce the changes hypothesized in H1–H6. The study's design can speak to this debate by testing whether, in the specific and novel domain of AI-generated content, individual-level interventions nonetheless produce measurable effects on detection accuracy, confidence, and trust, or whether the null results anticipated by the i-frame critique hold.

Retrieved works (OpenAlex; queries: inoculation intervention detection accuracy misinformation false content; accuracy nudge trust online information media literacy intervention effect; inoculation backfire effect overconfidence detection accuracy null; intervention transfer domain specificity AI-generated content detection distinct misinformation; survey experiment multiple treatment arms detection accuracy Lin estimator regression adjustment):

- Stephan Lewandowsky, Ullrich K. H. Ecker, John Cook (2017). Beyond misinformation: Understanding and coping with the “post-truth” era.. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jarmac.2017.07.008

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

# Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

*Yamil Velez · 2026-10-04 · N = 2,030 analysed of 2,257 collected · survey experiment*

![provenance: fully agentic](figures/badges/provenance.svg) ![review: 9/11 claims supported](figures/badges/review.svg) [![plan: pre-registered #151,281](figures/badges/registration.svg)](https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf) ![status: draft](figures/badges/release.svg) ![design: survey experiment](figures/badges/design.svg) ![data: open data](figures/badges/data.svg) ![model calls: $0.00](figures/badges/cost.svg)

[Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/ai-discernment

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A survey experiment with 11 arms and a control group; online panel, United States. 2,257 responses were collected and 2,030 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A survey experiment on online panel respondents in United States (N = 2,030 analysed). Respondents are randomly assigned to 12 arms: Flagging, Provenance, Automated Flagging, AI Accuracy Nudge, Breathing Exercise, Mindfulness, Inoculation, AI Literacy Infographic, AI Literacy Infographic 2, AI Literacy Guide, AI Text Video, against the control group Control. Flagging: Posts in the feed are flagged as potentially AI-generated. Provenance: Posts carry information about the content's source and origin (provenance). Automated Flagging: Posts carry machine-learning-based AI-detection labels (automated flagging). AI Accuracy Nudge: Before the feed, an interactive task asks 'Is this image AI-generated?' (accuracy nudge). Breathing Exercise: Before the feed, a box-breathing exercise to reduce emotional reactivity. Mindfulness: Before the feed, a short mindfulness exercise. Inoculation: Before the feed, an inoculation message pre-exposing the respondent to manipulation techniques used in AI-generated media. AI Literacy Infographic: Before the feed, an infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Infographic 2: Before the feed, an alternative infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Guide: Before the feed, a comprehensive guide with examples of AI artifacts in images and videos. AI Text Video: Before the feed, an educational video about AI-generated text. Outcomes: Accuracy (share of 24 posts judged correctly), AI attitudes (opportunity vs threat, 6 items), Confidence in AI detection (single 7-point item), Trust in online information (7 items).


The study was registered on AsPredicted (#151,281, 2023-11-15). Some data existed at registration, but later batches followed the plan. Of 2,257 raw respondents, 2,030 entered the analysis (227 excluded; the exclusion criteria and the split by arm are not in the tables). Outcome models dropped a few rows with missing values, so some arm sizes fall slightly below eligible counts. The control group had 181 respondents. Arms were unbalanced, from 78 (Inoculation) to 333 (AI Accuracy Nudge). All tests are two-sided and uncorrected for multiple comparisons.

*Pre-registered.*

## Related work

Prior findings relevant to the study's hypotheses are limited and mostly indirect. Lewandowsky et al. (2017) and Wang et al. (2019) document that misinformation spreads widely and that people are poor at identifying false claims, providing general support for the premise that detection accuracy (H1) and trust in online information (H4) are malleable and in need of intervention. Pluviano et al. (2020) show that source expertise and trustworthiness cues shape recollection of misinformation, which is tangentially relevant to H1 and H4 but does not address AI-generated content specifically. No retrieved work directly examines interventions aimed at detecting AI-generated text or posts, so the list is thin for the study's core domain.

The most pointed disagreement in the retrieved set concerns whether individual-level interventions can meaningfully shift information-processing outcomes. Chater and Loewenstein (2022) argue that focusing on individual-level solutions has led behavioral public policy astray, implying that the study's design—targeting individual participants with brief interventions—may be insufficient to produce the changes hypothesized in H1–H6. The study's design can speak to this debate by testing whether, in the specific and novel domain of AI-generated content, individual-level interventions nonetheless produce measurable effects on detection accuracy, confidence, and trust, or whether the null results anticipated by the i-frame critique hold.

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'mechanism'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Signal-detection re-test of Automated Flagging with per-post responses
Question: Does Automated Flagging improve discernment (d') for AI vs authentic media, or only shift the tendency to answer 'AI'?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes measurement: it records each post's response so d' and criterion can be computed, which settles U1; it also enlarges the sample for the only robust effect.
Design sketch: Arms: control, Automated Flagging, Breathing Exercise, AI Accuracy Nudge (the exploratory AI-post gainers). Each respondent judges 24 posts, 12 AI and 12 real, with per-post AI/real responses and a confidence rating. Add a 7-day follow-up on a fresh set of posts. Analyse d' and criterion by arm. Recruit a US online panel with a balanced allocation.
Power target: about 400 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (Observed Automated Flagging effect of 0.032 to 0.044 (H1a/H1); the table's MDE is 0.042 at n=127 vs 181, so about 400 per arm detects about 3 points.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Individual-level interventions vs system-level change): (a) Brief individual-level interventions (labels, nudges, literacy training) can improve people's handling of misleading content. versus (b) Focusing on individual-level fixes misdirects policy; system-level change is needed because the individual effects are small or fragile.. The source study says: It leans toward B for education and priming arms (pooled +1.0 point, CI [-0.3, 2.4]). The one robust effect comes from a platform-level cue (Automated Flagging), which is closer to a system change. The study cannot test the policy claim directly because it measures only immediate effects.
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U1

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

Limitations: Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

value.title: Signal-detection re-test of Automated Flagging with per-post responses
value.rationale: The source study reported Automated Flagging raising accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]) and exploratory gains in AI-post detection for Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge, but only share-correct scores exist, so discernment cannot be separated from a bias to answer 'AI'. Recording each post's response allows d' and criterion to be computed, and a 7-day follow-up checks whether effects persist.
value.contribution: Separates true discernment (d') from response bias (criterion) for the one robust platform-level cue versus two individual-level interventions, informing the individual versus system-level debate.

Follow-up posts are a different set, so item difficulty may differ
Online US panel; stimulus set drawn from the source study's style of posts
Four arms only; other source arms are not retested

design.title: Signal-detection re-test of Automated Flagging
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to control, Automated Flagging, Breathing Exercise or AI Accuracy Nudge. They judge 24 posts (12 AI, 12 real) as AI or real and rate confidence on each. Seven days later they judge a fresh set of 24 posts without any intervention cue. d' and criterion are computed per respondent.
design.hypothesis: Automated Flagging raises d' relative to control; Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge shift criterion toward answering 'AI' without raising d'.
design.primaryOutcome: d' (z(hit rate) minus z(false alarm rate)) across the 24 posts, with criterion as the secondary outcome.
design.comparison: Each treatment arm versus control on d' and criterion, at the immediate session and at the 7-day follow-up.
design.population: US adults from an online panel, balanced allocation across arms, about 400 per arm.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. ## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

Limitations: Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

function.name: record_result
function.description: Hand a structured result to the orchestrator. Set final=true when your task is complete.

value.title: Where flagging works: media type and baseline literacy
value.rationale: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004) in one US online panel, with 181 controls and no pre-planned moderator. This 2 x 3 test asks whether the effect holds for images, video and text-only posts, and across baseline AI knowledge and media trust. Per-post responses are also recorded, so sensitivity and false-alarm rates can be separated.
value.contribution: Tests whether the Automated Flagging effect generalises across media formats and baseline AI knowledge in a quota sample.
limitations: Interactions are underpowered by design; they are pre-registered but should be read as estimates.
Text-only posts are not the same as the image and video stimuli of the source study, so format is confounded with content.
Effects are measured immediately after exposure in an online panel.
Self-reported AI knowledge is a coarse proxy for literacy.

design.title: Automated Flagging across media formats and baseline literacy
design.overview: Respondents give consent and answer pre-treatment measures of AI knowledge and media trust. They are then randomised to a format (image, video or text-only) and to control or Automated Flagging. They judge 12 posts in that format as AI-generated or authentic, and then answer the source confidence item.
design.hypothesis: H1: Automated Flagging raises accuracy in every format. H2: The effect differs by format. H3: The effect differs by baseline AI knowledge and media trust.
design.primaryOutcome: Share of 12 posts correctly classified as AI-generated or authentic.
design.comparison: Automated Flagging vs control within each format, and interactions with format, AI knowledge and media trust.
design.population: US adults from an online panel, with quotas balanced on age and education.

conditions.description: Posts are shown without labels.

conditions.title: Automated Flagging
conditions.description: Each post carries a machine-learning AI-detection label.

assumptions: Target about 450 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power; pooled Automated Flagging was about 0.032 to 0.044, so each format-by-condition cell needs about 450 to detect a 3-point effect; interactions are underpowered by design.
Six cells of about 450 give roughly 2,700 respondents.
The sample is a US online panel with quotas on age and education.
Compensation follows panel norms for a 10-minute survey.
The 12 posts per respondent are shown as a sequence in one format; each post has a judgment question, and the stimulus set is built in the platform.

The randomizer nests format first and then condition; this gives equal allocation across the six cells.
Interactions with AI knowledge and media trust are pre-registered.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'alternative'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (survey_experiment). Title: Source of the flagging benefit: label accuracy vs mere cueing
Question: Do labels help because they carry valid information (an individual-level cue) or because any warning shifts the response criterion?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes design: the original arms confounded label presence with label validity, so it cannot say which position fits the data.
Design sketch: Arms: no label; valid automated labels (about 85% accurate); random labels with the same base rate; a generic 'be careful' banner. Use per-post responses and compute d' and criterion. If only valid labels raise d', the benefit comes from platform information, supporting B. If random labels give the same lift, the effect is a bias shift from a cue. Add a trust-in-labels measure.
Power target: about 400 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (Automated Flagging observed +0.032 to +0.044 against an MDE of 0.042 at n=127; 400 per arm sizes it to 3 points.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Individual-level interventions vs system-level change): (a) Brief individual-level interventions (labels, nudges, literacy training) can improve people's handling of misleading content. versus (b) Focusing on individual-level fixes misdirects policy; system-level change is needed because the individual effects are small or fragile.. The source study says: It leans toward B for education and priming arms (pooled +1.0 point, CI [-0.3, 2.4]). The one robust effect comes from a platform-level cue (Automated Flagging), which is closer to a system change. The study cannot test the policy claim directly because it measures only immediate effects.
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U1

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

Limitations: Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

value.rationale: Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]) while the pooled effect of other arms was +1.0 point (CI [-0.3, 2.4]), but label presence was confounded with label validity. design.title: Valid vs random labels vs generic warning
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to one of four arms and judge 24 posts (12 AI, 12 authentic) as AI or not AI. Arms: no label, valid automated labels (about 85% accurate), random labels with the same base rate of 'AI' labels, or a generic 'be careful' banner. Signal-detection d' and criterion are computed per respondent from per-post responses.
design.hypothesis: Only valid labels raise d' relative to no label (information account). If random labels or the banner shift criterion without raising d', the benefit is a cue-driven bias shift.
design.primaryOutcome: Per-respondent d' computed from 24 per-post AI/not-AI judgments; criterion c is secondary.
design.comparison: Valid labels vs no label on d'; valid vs random labels on d'; random labels and banner vs no label on criterion.
design.population: US adults from an online panel, about 400 per arm (1,600 total).

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'alternative'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (survey_experiment). Title: Source of the flagging benefit: label accuracy vs mere cueing
Question: Do labels help because they carry valid information (an individual-level cue) or because any warning shifts the response criterion?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes design: the original arms confounded label presence with label validity, so it cannot say which position fits the data.
Design sketch: Arms: no label; valid automated labels (about 85% accurate); random labels with the same base rate; a generic 'be careful' banner. Use per-post responses and compute d' and criterion. If only valid labels raise d', the benefit comes from platform information, supporting B. If random labels give the same lift, the effect is a bias shift from a cue. Add a trust-in-labels measure.
Power target: about 400 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (Automated Flagging observed +0.032 to +0.044 against an MDE of 0.042 at n=127; 400 per arm sizes it to 3 points.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Individual-level interventions vs system-level change): (a) Brief individual-level interventions (labels, nudges, literacy training) can improve people's handling of misleading content. versus (b) Focusing on individual-level fixes misdirects policy; system-level change is needed because the individual effects are small or fragile.. The source study says: It leans toward B for education and priming arms (pooled +1.0 point, CI [-0.3, 2.4]). The one robust effect comes from a platform-level cue (Automated Flagging), which is closer to a system change. The study cannot test the policy claim directly because it measures only immediate effects.
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U1

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

Limitations: Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

## Abstract

Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A survey experiment with 11 arms and a control group; online panel, United States. 2,257 responses were collected and 2,030 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/q2eh95.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A survey experiment on online panel respondents in United States (N = 2,030 analysed). Respondents are randomly assigned to 12 arms: Flagging, Provenance, Automated Flagging, AI Accuracy Nudge, Breathing Exercise, Mindfulness, Inoculation, AI Literacy Infographic, AI Literacy Infographic 2, AI Literacy Guide, AI Text Video, against the control group Control. Flagging: Posts in the feed are flagged as potentially AI-generated. Provenance: Posts carry information about the content's source and origin (provenance). Automated Flagging: Posts carry machine-learning-based AI-detection labels (automated flagging). AI Accuracy Nudge: Before the feed, an interactive task asks 'Is this image AI-generated?' (accuracy nudge). Breathing Exercise: Before the feed, a box-breathing exercise to reduce emotional reactivity. Mindfulness: Before the feed, a short mindfulness exercise. Inoculation: Before the feed, an inoculation message pre-exposing the respondent to manipulation techniques used in AI-generated media. AI Literacy Infographic: Before the feed, an infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Infographic 2: Before the feed, an alternative infographic on how to identify AI-generated content. AI Literacy Guide: Before the feed, a comprehensive guide with examples of AI artifacts in images and videos. AI Text Video: Before the feed, an educational video about AI-generated text. Outcomes: Accuracy (share of 24 posts judged correctly), AI attitudes (opportunity vs threat, 6 items), Confidence in AI detection (single 7-point item), Trust in online information (7 items).


The study was registered on AsPredicted (#151,281, 2023-11-15). Some data existed at registration, but later batches followed the plan. Of 2,257 raw respondents, 2,030 entered the analysis (227 excluded; the exclusion criteria and the split by arm are not in the tables). Outcome models dropped a few rows with missing values, so some arm sizes fall slightly below eligible counts. The control group had 181 respondents. Arms were unbalanced, from 78 (Inoculation) to 333 (AI Accuracy Nudge). All tests are two-sided and uncorrected for multiple comparisons.

## Related work

Prior findings relevant to the study's hypotheses are limited and mostly indirect. Lewandowsky et al. (2017) and Wang et al. (2019) document that misinformation spreads widely and that people are poor at identifying false claims, providing general support for the premise that detection accuracy (H1) and trust in online information (H4) are malleable and in need of intervention. Pluviano et al. (2020) show that source expertise and trustworthiness cues shape recollection of misinformation, which is tangentially relevant to H1 and H4 but does not address AI-generated content specifically. No retrieved work directly examines interventions aimed at detecting AI-generated text or posts, so the list is thin for the study's core domain.

The most pointed disagreement in the retrieved set concerns whether individual-level interventions can meaningfully shift information-processing outcomes. Chater and Loewenstein (2022) argue that focusing on individual-level solutions has led behavioral public policy astray, implying that the study's design—targeting individual participants with brief interventions—may be insufficient to produce the changes hypothesized in H1–H6. The study's design can speak to this debate by testing whether, in the specific and novel domain of AI-generated content, individual-level interventions nonetheless produce measurable effects on detection accuracy, confidence, and trust, or whether the null results anticipated by the i-frame critique hold.

## Limitations

Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'mechanism'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Discernment vs response bias in AI labels
Question: Does Automated Flagging improve true discernment (d') or only shift willingness to answer 'AI'?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes measurement: computes sensitivity and criterion from AI and real post responses, and adds confidence ratings.
Design sketch: Arms: control, Automated Flagging, and Automated Flagging with a stated label error rate (e.g. 80% accurate). Each respondent judges 24 posts, half AI-generated, with a per-item confidence rating. Outcomes are d' and criterion, plus a sharing intention. Recruit a US online panel.
Power target: about 400 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (Observed Automated Flagging effect 0.032 to 0.044 on total accuracy; H1 MDE at n=127/181 was 0.042; n=400/arm gives about 0.028 for SD 0.13.); record it in design.assumptions

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

Limitations: Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. ## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'generalizability_conditional')
Type: generalizability_conditional (survey_experiment). Title: Label effect by label reliability and prior AI skill
Question: Does the Automated Flagging benefit hold when labels are imperfect and across respondents with different AI familiarity?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the sample and missing-moderator causes by testing where the one robust effect holds.
Design sketch: Randomise label reliability (95% vs 70% accurate) crossed with a control, using video and image stimuli. Stratify recruitment by the AI-familiarity scale (ai_scale). Outcome is accuracy on both AI and real posts.
Moderator or condition whose variation the design must cover: Label reliability and AI familiarity (ai_scale), with stimulus type (image vs video)
Power target: about 350 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (Observed Automated Flagging +0.032 raw; n=350/arm gives MDE about 0.03 at SD 0.13.); record it in design.assumptions

## Source study
Title: Improving AI Discernment: do misinformation interventions help people spot AI-generated media?

Abstract: Can brief misinformation interventions help people tell AI-generated media from authentic media? We ran a registered online survey experiment in the United States (fielded October to November 2023). Of 2,257 respondents collected, 2,030 were analysed; they were randomised to a control (n=181) or one of 11 interventions, then judged posts in a simulated feed. Pooled across arms, total accuracy was not distinguishable from control (+1.0 point, 95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]). Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]). The AI Literacy Guide (+4.7 points) and Mindfulness (−3.9 points) are borderline adjusted estimates that the raw means do not reproduce, so they are tentative. Several arms shifted confidence or attitudes. With about 44 uncorrected arm-level tests and some small arms, isolated effects near the threshold should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Across 11 interventions, the registered tests found no clear overall gain in total accuracy; the pooled estimate was +1.0 point (95% CI [−0.3, +2.4]).
- Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004). The AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points is tentative, borderline and model-dependent (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]).
- Mindfulness's adjusted estimate of −3.9 points on total accuracy (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]) is borderline, and the raw means do not reproduce it. Flagging and AI Literacy Infographic 2 lowered confidence in AI detection.
- Exploratory: the Breathing Exercise and AI Accuracy Nudge raised the share of AI posts identified. This may reflect a greater tendency to answer 'AI' rather than better discernment.
- Main caveat: about 44 registered arm-level tests were uncorrected, several arms are small, and some adjusted estimates depend on the model rather than raw means.

Limitations: Many arm-level tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons: 44 registered and 22 post hoc. A few significant results are about what chance would produce, and several sit near p = 0.05. Some adjusted estimates (the Guide, Mindfulness, Breathing Exercise) are not reproduced by raw means. Some arms are small (78 to 102 respondents), so their intervals are wide. The splits for AI-generated and authentic posts (H5, H6) are post hoc. The sample is an online U.S. panel, effects were measured right after a brief exposure, and part of the data predates registration.

function.description: Hand a structured result to the orchestrator. Set final=true when your task is complete.

value.title: Label effect by label reliability and prior AI skill
value.rationale: Automated Flagging was the one robust gain (+4.4 points, 95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p=0.004; control n=181 of 2,030 analysed), but the labels' accuracy was not varied and no moderator such as AI familiarity was tested. This design tests whether the benefit holds when labels are 95% versus 70% accurate, across AI familiarity levels, and for images versus videos.
value.contribution: Maps the conditions (label reliability, AI familiarity, media type) under which automated AI labels improve discernment on both AI and real posts.
limitations: Labels are simulated, not real detector outputs.
Short post-exposure task on an online panel; 12 posts limit stimulus-level precision.
Familiarity is self-reported and the strata are approximate.
Power targets the main effect (MDE about 0.03), not the interactions.

design.title: Automated labels: reliability, AI familiarity and media type
design.overview: Respondents report AI familiarity, then are randomised to no labels, labels that are 95% accurate, or labels that are 70% accurate. They judge 12 posts (6 images, 6 videos; half AI-generated, half real) and say whether each is AI-generated. Recruitment is stratified by AI familiarity.
design.hypothesis: Labels at 95% accuracy raise accuracy over control; labels at 70% accuracy raise it less or not at all, and may lower accuracy on posts the labels mislabel. The benefit is larger for low-familiarity respondents.
design.primaryOutcome: Share of posts judged correctly, reported separately for AI posts and real posts, and by image versus video.
design.comparison: Each label arm versus control; 95% versus 70% accuracy; interaction with ai_scale tercile and with media type.
design.population: US online panel adults, stratified into low, medium and high AI familiarity based on the ai_scale screener.
